# Arbitrary finite bases: upward max propagation gives exact compatible erosions

This proves an actual simultaneous deformation, not a cap-signature
identity or an asserted optimal continuation. It propagates prescribed
source fields through finitely many anchored relations, uses their
pointwise maximum where demands meet, and gives exact convex fibers for
all sufficiently small positive parameters. The resulting cost can be
exponential even on a product interval; no parity budget is asserted.

Throughout, `d>=1`. All continuous fibers have positive `d`-volume.
The construction is independent of criticality. Critical caps enter
only in the final fixed-cover payment test, with their original masses
and actual full/empty/proper statuses retained.

## 1. Finite actual anchored relations and an acyclic assignment

Let `P` be a finite set of distinct points in `Z^n` satisfying

    conv(P) intersect Z^n = P.

Let `K_z` be compact positive convex bodies in `R^d`, for `z in P`, with
the actual compatibility property

    sum_z lambda_z K_z subset K_q
    whenever lambda_z>=0, sum lambda_z=1, sum lambda_z z=q in P.    (1)

For example these are the positive fibers of a convex body after taking
their fiber hull and removing volume-zero fibers by the established
positive-fiber reduction. The theorem can also simply assume (1).

For each `q`, let `R_q` be the finite vertex set of the compact polytope

    Lambda_q={lambda>=0: sum lambda=1, sum lambda_z z=q}.

The vertex `delta_q` is the self representation. Every other vertex has
`lambda_q=0`: a representation with `0<lambda_q<1` is the nontrivial
convex combination of `delta_q` and its normalized remainder. In
particular every nonself vertex has at least two positive inputs.

Choose a linear height `ell` taking distinct values on `P`, and order
the bases by increasing height. At each nonself extreme relation
`e=(q,lambda)`, choose a positive input `z(e)` with

    ell(z(e)) > ell(q).                                      (2)

Such an input exists, since `ell(q)` is the weighted average of the
distinct input heights. All directed edges `q -> z(e)` therefore point
strictly upward. Their graph has no cycle. No geometric assertion that
contact cells are disjoint or have smaller affine dimension is used.

## 2. The transfer operator and the pointwise least propagated fields

Prescribe finite nonnegative fields

    F_z:S^(d-1) times R^d -> [0,infinity)

continuous jointly in normal and physical point, and convex in the
physical point for each fixed normal. A field may be identically zero.
For a nonself extreme relation `e=(q,lambda)` with charged input `z`, set

    (T_e V)(n,x)
       = (1/lambda_z) sup_{x_j in K_j, j!=z, lambda_j>0}
              V(n,lambda_z x + sum_{j!=z}lambda_j x_j).       (3)

The supremum is over a fixed compact set. Thus `T_e V` is finite on
compact sets, continuous jointly in `(n,x)`, nonnegative, and convex in
`x`. Continuity follows directly from uniform continuity of `V` on the
compact set swept out by convergent `(n,x)` and all the partner points;
no measurable optimizer is needed. The operator is monotone and obeys

    T_e max(V_1,...,V_r)=max(T_e V_1,...,T_e V_r).             (4)

Initialize `V_z=F_z`. Process bases in increasing height. When processing
`q`, its field is already final, since no later edge can return to it.
For each extreme relation at `q`, update its charged input by

    V_z <- max(V_z,T_e V_q).                                 (5)

There are finitely many such updates. Every final field retains the
continuity, nonnegativity and physical convexity above, and satisfies

    V_z>=F_z,     V_{z(e)}>=T_e V_q for every assigned edge.  (6)

These final fields are pointwise least among all fields satisfying (6)
for this chosen height and edge assignment. This follows by induction
over the height order using monotonicity of `T_e`. Equivalently, by (4),
`V_z` is the maximum over all directed seed-to-`z` paths of the composed
transfers applied to that path's seed field, including the path of
length zero. All paths have length at most `|P|-1`.

This least-field statement concerns the sufficient one-input demands
(6). It does NOT identify the least-cost compatible deformation. Actual
compatibility may use several input fields together, whereas (3)
deliberately makes one input pay the whole target demand.

## 3. Exact convex bodies, all representations, and the actual hull

Write `h_z(n)=h_{K_z}(n)` and define

    K_z(epsilon)={x: n.x+epsilon V_z(n,x)<=h_z(n)
                         for every unit normal n}.          (7)

For all sufficiently small `epsilon>=0`, these are positive compact
convex bodies, nested inside `K_z`. Indeed choose `o_z in int K_z`.
On a compact neighborhood of `K_z`, the ratio
`V_z(n,x)/h_{K_z-o_z}(n)` is uniformly bounded by some `C_z`.
For small epsilon,

    o_z+(1-C_z epsilon)(K_z-o_z)
             subset K_z(epsilon) subset K_z.                (8)

The first inclusion follows by inserting its points in (7); the second
uses nonnegativity. Physical convexity of `V_z` makes every defining
sublevel convex. Compactness follows from the second inclusion.

Fix a nonself extreme representation `(q,lambda)` and arbitrary input
points `x_j in K_j(epsilon)`. Put `m=sum lambda_j x_j`. Since these
points also belong to the original partner bodies, (3) and (6) give

    sum_j lambda_j V_j(n,x_j)
       >=lambda_{z(e)}V_{z(e)}(n,x_{z(e)}) >= V_q(n,m).

Consequently the input inequalities and the original compatibility
yield, for every normal,

    n.m+epsilon V_q(n,m)
       <=sum_j lambda_j h_j(n) <=h_q(n).

Thus `m in K_q(epsilon)`. The self representation is immediate.

This also proves every nonextreme representation, without assuming
support-function convexity of the new fields. Write its coefficient
vector as `lambda=sum_r a_r lambda^r` in extreme representations and,
using the same input points, put `m_r=sum_z lambda_z^r x_z`. Each `m_r`
belongs to `K_q(epsilon)`; their convex combination is `m`. Hence

    sum_z lambda_z K_z(epsilon) subset K_q(epsilon)           (9)

for EVERY anchored representation in (1).

Finally let

    C_epsilon=conv union_{z in P} ({z} times K_z(epsilon)).   (10)

Grouping points of any convex combination by their integer base and
then applying (9) proves that its fiber at each `q in P` is exactly
`K_q(epsilon)`. Its projection remains `conv(P)` by nonemptiness, and
lattice completeness implies it has no other integer bases. This is
therefore an actual relative convex-body deformation with precisely the
stated mixed measure, full dimensional in `aff(P) times R^d`. It lies
inside the original fiber hull. Replacing an
original body by its fiber hull at epsilon zero changes no positive
integer fiber, mixed mass, or mixed halfspace depth.

If a full-dimensional ambient convex body in `R^(n+d)` is required when
`rank aff(P)<n`, it can be supplied without changing any integer fiber.
Choose `p_0 in P`, let `V=span(P-p_0)`, and let `pi` be orthogonal
projection onto `V^perp`. Since `V` is spanned by integer vectors, the
matrix of `pi` is rational, so `pi(Z^n)` is a discrete subgroup of
`(1/N)Z^n` for some positive integer `N`. Its nonzero vectors have a
positive minimum length `rho`. Add to every body (10) the SAME closed
ball of radius `eta<rho` in `V^perp times {0}`. An integer base `z` of
this thickening has perpendicular displacement `pi(z-p_0)` of length
at most `eta`; discreteness forces that displacement to be zero. Its
base therefore belongs to `conv(P) intersect Z^n=P`, and its added
perpendicular component is zero, so its fiber is unchanged. These
thickenings are nested full-dimensional ambient bodies. They need not
lie inside an originally supplied full-dimensional body; the mixed sets
are still exactly the nested sets already proved above. If `V=R^n`,
no thickening is needed.

All conclusions above are exact at small positive epsilon. They use no
polyhedral approximation, infinitesimal contact repair, or assumed
smoothness of the fibers.

## 4. Nonsmooth first variations and fixed closed-cap selectors

The continuum-normal first-variation theorem proved in Section 3 of
`candidate c56743c8d6824a18`
applies to the final fields, including their maxima and their zeros. It
gives

    |K_z|-|K_z(epsilon)|=epsilon D_z+o(epsilon),
    D_z=integral_{boundary K_z} V_z(n_z(x),x) dH^(d-1)(x).  (11)

Here `n_z` is the unique outward unit normal at surface-almost every
boundary point. For completeness, after translating by an interior
point, (8) uniformly bounds the fractional radial loss. At a radial
endpoint `x`, that fractional loss divided by epsilon tends to

    max_{n supporting at x} V_z(n,x)/h_{K_z-o_z}(n).

Compactness of the normal sphere proves this by selecting an active
constraint; nonunique normal cones are surface-null. Radial dominated
convergence and the cone Jacobian give (11). This also covers `d=1`
with counting boundary measure.

For a fixed original ambient closed halfspace `H`, use its ACTUAL
restriction `H_z` at base `z`, including the original integer tilt.
Define the boundary loss selector

    kappa_{z,H}(x)=1_{int H_z}(x) if H_z cuts K_z properly;
                  1 if K_z subset H_z;
                  0 if int K_z intersect H_z is empty.      (12)

Inside and outside supporting coincidences have respectively the full
and zero statuses in (12). A proper cut meets the fiber boundary along
a surface-null set, since this intersection is the relative boundary
of its full-dimensional hyperplane section. Thus

    mu(H)-mu_epsilon(H)=epsilon D(H)+o(epsilon),
    D(H)=sum_z integral_{boundary K_z} kappa_{z,H} V_z dS,
    M-M_epsilon=epsilon D+o(epsilon), D=sum_z D_z.           (13)

Purely integer halfspaces have only full or zero traces, with a fiber
on their closed boundary included in FULL. A closed outside supporting
facet must not be assigned fictitious loss by its boundary indicator.
For any fixed finite menu the little-o terms in (13) are uniform simply
because the menu is finite.

The integrand in (11)--(13) is the ACTUAL final maximum from (5). It is
not the sum of the costs of its paths or incoming demands. Overlapping
demands are charged once on the physical boundary.

## 5. Projective seeds and the precise surviving source credit

At a selected source `Y_i=(p_i,y_i)`, with `y_i in int K_{p_i}`, choose
the ordinary projective normalizer `a_i` of `K_{p_i}-y_i`, and the finite
positive convex tangent extension `f_i` of `t^(-d)`. Its source field is

    P_i(n,x)=h_{K_{p_i}-y_i}(n) f_i(1+a_i.(x-y_i)).         (14)

The projective theorem in
`candidate 4e871da0351ca07a`
gives its prescribed total cost

    d_i=integral_{boundary K_{p_i}}P_i dS
       =d |T_{a_i}(K_{p_i}-y_i)| >0,                       (15)

and loss at least `Gamma_d d_i` in every closed halfspace through `y_i`.
The same lower bound holds for a containing cap by including its
parallel through-source cap. Full traces lose `d_i`, which is larger.

Use `F_p=max_{i:p_i=p}P_i`, with zero at unassigned bases. Then final
`V_p>=P_i`, and every actual ambient halfspace containing `Y_i` obeys

    D_{p_i}(H)>=Gamma_d d_i.                                (16)

For sources on distinct bases their contributions add in `D(H)`. If
several sources share one base, only the maximum of the applicable
individual lower bounds is automatic; their seeds share the same
boundary and must not be summed as disjoint mass.

Crucially, (16) involves the prescribed projective cost `d_i`, NOT the
possibly larger final own-fiber cost `D_{p_i}`. Incoming demands can
raise that cost with loss outside this cap. No inequality
`D_{p_i}(H)>=Gamma_d D_{p_i}` follows merely from `V_{p_i}>=P_i`.
All additional cap losses remain in the exact formula (13), as do all
additional volume costs.

## 6. A precise finite-cover descent test

Suppose a finite collection of original ambient halfspaces covers the
original mixed set, each has mass at most the actual maximal raw depth
`Q`, and write `beta=Q/M`. Split it into its critical rows of mass `Q`
and its rows with strict mass slack. If the constructed fields satisfy

    R_H := D(H)-beta D >0
    for EVERY critical row in this fixed cover,             (17)

then the actual family (10) has strictly smaller global normalized
depth for all sufficiently small positive epsilon.

Indeed the old cover still covers the nested new mixed set. For a
critical row, (13) gives normalized mass

    beta-epsilon R_H/M+o(epsilon).

The finite critical set has a positive minimum surplus; the other
finite rows preserve their strict gaps. Every possible new center is
therefore controlled. This is a sufficient fixed-cover test. It does
not assert the test always passes, replace the actual menu by unrelated
per-source caps, interchange menu choices with allocations, or rule out
another descent when this particular test fails.

When a fixed witness circuit covers its entire fiber plane and the
remaining bases have persistent slack covers, these covers supply the
hypothesis above. The construction itself does not prove that cover
interface or its parity witness-count theorem anew.

## 7. Exact exponential-cost calibration on a complete interval

Let `P={-m,...,m}` with `m>=1`, all fibers equal to a positive convex
body `L` with centroid zero, and prescribe the single central projective
seed `F_0(n,x)=h_L(n)`. All other seeds are zero. Use increasing base
height and charge each nonself extreme relation to its higher input.

The nonself extreme representations of `q` are exactly the bracketing
pairs `i<q<j`, with higher-input coefficient `(q-i)/(j-i)`. Every
propagated field is constant in `x` and has the form `g_q h_L(n)`. The
algorithm gives EXACTLY

    g_q=0 for q<0,       g_q=2^q for q>=0.                  (18)

For the upper bound, the transfer `q -> j` from a nonnegative `q` is

    2^q (j-i)/(q-i)
       <=2^q (1+j-q) <=2^j,

because `q-i` is a positive integer. Negative targets have zero fields.
For attainment, each adjacent relation
`q=(q-1+q+1)/2` transfers `2g_q`, starting at `g_0=1`.
This proves (18) by induction, including every nonadjacent demand.

The actual eroded bodies are `(1-epsilon g_q)L`. Their total first cost
and prescribed source cost have ratio

    D/d_0=sum_{q=0}^m 2^q=2^(m+1)-1.                       (19)

The equal-field continuation `V_q=h_L` at all bases is also compatible
and costs only `(2m+1)d_0`: it uses both inputs' existing credit instead
of requiring one input to fund an entire target. Thus the acyclic
construction is intentionally conservative, despite its exact
pointwise max sharing. Neither its cost nor its total-cost/source-cost
ratio is bounded by the two occupied parities. This example makes no
negative statement about its SAME-cap input credits in (13).

## 8. Relation to the archived mechanisms

The one-relation case is the worst-partner one-input erosion proved in
Section 7 of
`candidate c56743c8d6824a18`.
The new extension is the finite acyclic propagation across ALL anchored
relations, with the least pointwise maximum of coincident demands and
exact fiber-hull realization on an arbitrary complete base.

This is different from
`candidate c7b6ab042f325988`
and `candidate 046287857a52d424`:
those retain common-source laws or removed-shell signatures and their
cap credits, rather than constructing this system of nonlinear convex
erosion inequalities. It also does not duplicate the signed affine-jet
Farkas identity in
`candidate f2040d65ee0d1d9e`:
the present containments hold exactly at finite small parameters and
need no hull repair of second-order errors.

Finally the product continuation cost obstruction in
`candidate 22d923b6274e7758`
already warns against a parity bound on denominator cost alone. Equation
(19) adds the exact cost of this particular upward one-input algorithm,
not a new universal lower bound. The missing quantitative payment is
still the actual signed cover inequality (17), with input credits kept.

## 9. Maxima of independently compatible arrays: an intersection theorem

There is a useful stronger closure fact, suggested by the parent audit.
Suppose finitely many continuous nonnegative convex-in-`x` field arrays
`V_z^r` on the SAME original fibers each define actual compatible families
by (7), for every sufficiently small positive epsilon. They need not
have been produced by one height order, or even satisfy the pointwise
one-input bounds (6). Then

    V_z=max_r V_z^r                                          (20)

also defines an actual compatible family. Indeed its new fiber is
exactly `intersection_r K_z^r(epsilon)`. For any anchored relation,

    sum lambda_z intersection_r K_z^r(epsilon)
       subset intersection_r sum lambda_z K_z^r(epsilon)
       subset intersection_r K_q^r(epsilon).

The fibers remain positive for small epsilon by the common inner
homothet estimate (8). Alternatively one can intersect the actual
convex bodies of the finitely many deformations: its integer fibers are
these intersections, and all bases remain occupied. Taking their fiber
hull gives the same integer fibers as before. There is no assertion that
intersection commutes with convex hull at noninteger bases.

The first losses are therefore the integrals of `max_r V_z^r`, with the
same exact selectors (12). In particular different upward height orders
can be combined by a maximum, not merely different incoming demands
within a single order. This conclusion uses actual convex intersection
and does not presume a Jensen inequality for an arbitrary field array.

This closure does not automatically preserve positive normalized
payment. For two arrays, the exact pointwise identity
`max(V,W)=V+W-min(V,W)` gives, for each fixed cap row,

    R_H(max(V,W))=R_H(V)+R_H(W)
       -sum_z integral (kappa_{z,H}-beta) min(V_z,W_z) dS.   (21)

The sign of the shared credit in (21) must be retained. For arrays from
Sections 1--3, their sum is also compatible by adding their pointwise
anchored inequalities; for arbitrary compatible arrays only the maximum
closure has been established here. Equation (21) is an identity of
boundary losses in either case, not an unproved assertion about a sum
deformation. The exact multi-witness interval calibration is recorded
separately by Defect, including its selected-menu dependence.
